headline: Fleet and commercial vehicles get their own hall as Saudi freight operators scale
deck: A truck is the most expensive asset a logistics operator owns and the one whose utilisation is hardest to fix.
excerpt: Fleet and commercial vehicles sit among the declared segments at the Saudi Warehousing & Logistics Expo. For operators scaling into a market with 59 planned logistics zones, the vehicle purchase is the least reversible decision they make.
content:
Fleet and commercial vehicles are one of the declared segments at the Saudi Warehousing & Logistics Expo in Riyadh, alongside warehousing, cold chain, freight forwarding, last-mile delivery, multimodal transport and terminals.

They deserve the separate billing. For a logistics operator, the vehicle fleet is typically the largest capital item on the balance sheet and the one with the least flexibility once committed. A warehouse lease can be exited. A software contract can be replaced. A hundred tractor units bought against a five-year contract are a hundred tractor units for five years, and their residual value at the end of it is set by a market the operator does not control.

The specification decisions behind that purchase are unglamorous and consequential. Axle configuration determines what can be carried legally and where. Powertrain choice sets fuel cost, which in long-haul freight is the largest single operating line. Telematics determines whether the operator knows what the fleet is doing in enough detail to bill for it, to prove a temperature record, or to defend a delivery claim.

The utilisation question sits above all of it. A truck earns only while it is loaded and moving. Empty running is the industry's structural waste, and it is a network problem rather than a vehicle problem: it is created by imbalanced freight flows, which in Saudi Arabia means the movement of construction materials and imported goods inland from the ports with much less to carry back.

That imbalance is a feature of an economy that is building rather than exporting manufactured goods, and it is one of the quieter arguments for the industrial localisation programme. A factory in an inland industrial city that ships finished product back towards a port gives the return leg something to carry.

Maintenance is the other half of the utilisation equation and the one where market structure matters. A fleet operating between Riyadh, Jubail and Jeddah needs service capability at both ends of every route and a spares position that does not strand a vehicle for a week. That is a dealer network question, and it is the reason commercial vehicle competition in this region is fought on aftersales as much as on the vehicle.

The policy backdrop is a National Transport and Logistics Strategy targeting 59 logistics zones by 2030 across more than 100 million square metres, with the sector aimed at 10 per cent of gross domestic product. Zones generate freight, and freight generates fleet.

The expo runs at the Riyadh International Convention & Exhibition Center from 8 to 10 September, with more than 170 exhibitors showing over 3,500 products and services.
author: Jakson Gudawela
